newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW - Motorola plans new Brazil plants.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Motorola plans new Brazil plants.

text.p: U.S. technology giant Motorola Inc, positioning itself for a boom in Brazilian cellular telephone services, will start building two new factories in Brazil in 1997, the firm's local chief said.
"We are very probably going to start two new plants, one in the middle of the year and one at the end," said Flavio Grynszpan, president of Motorola do Brasil Ltda.
"This is part of a long-range project. Our plans are to grow with the market," Grynszpan added.

Anticipating exploding demand next year for cellular and other telecoms equipment, Motorola has bought a 200-acre lot near its existing Campinas plant in Sao Paulo state and plans to move its entire Brazil manufacturing operation there, he said.
"It's a big project. We are going to build a new center there," he said. "It's hard to estimate how much it will cost but it will very probably be many hundreds of millions of dollars."
The new Jaguariuna site is a half-mile from Motorola's existing plant.

Brazil plans next year to open up the cellular market to allow private investors to operate services on the B Band frequency as well as begin the break-up and selloff of federal telecoms giant Telebras TEL.SA.

Motorola, one of the world's largest manufacturers and suppliers of cellular equipment, had not decided yet exactly what products it will build at the new plant, saying it would depend on "market needs," Grynszpan said.

Today, it makes only cellular phones in Brazil. But it may expand operations to include manufacture and installation of base stations, digital Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) cellular systems and other products and services, he said.
Motorola saw brisk growth in Brazil this year, doubling its workforce to more than 300 employees from 1995, Grynszpan said.
"We expect to double that again next year," he said. "It's a natural experience for the company, because it's a global company, and given the experience of the region."
In recent years, privatizations of Latin American telecom firms have been followed by rapid expansion in demand for equipment and services as new operators strive to meet pent-up demand.
While Motorola do Brasil Ltda is mainly a supplier, its U.S.-based parent is eyeing the sell-off of B Band concessions to gain a foothold in Brazil's budding cellular market.

"We'll probably be an investor in a cellular consortium," he said. "We have a division in the United States that's interested in being an investor, a shareholder in providing telecommunications services."
